children.title: 1.1 Ridge regression
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.1 Ridge regression

children.title: 1.1.1 The singular value decomposition and principal components analysis
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.1 Ridge regression/1.1.1 The singular value decomposition and principal components analysis
children.summary: The section titled '1.1.1 The singular value decomposition and principal components analysis' introduces the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) as a generalization of eigendecomposition for any matrix X, defining its factorization into orthogonal matrices U and V and a diagonal matrix D containing singular values. It details the 'thin SVD' variant used when n ≥ p and applies this decomposition to derive the fitted values for ridge regression, demonstrating how it shrinks coordinates relative to Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). The text concludes by establishing the connection between SVD and Principal Components Analysis (PCA).

children.title: 1.2 v-fold cross-validation
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.2 v-fold cross-validation
children.summary: This page continues a mathematical derivation regarding ridge regression and principal components, specifically focusing on how the method shrinks Y in smaller principal components. It then introduces section 1.2, 'v-fold cross-validation,' explaining it as a technique for selecting optimal regression parameters (lambda) by splitting data into groups to estimate prediction error.

children.title: 1.3 The kernel trick
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.3 The kernel trick
children.summary: The section titled '1.3 The kernel trick' explains a computational method to efficiently handle non-linear models, specifically ridge regression with quadratic effects. It demonstrates that by reformulating the problem to depend only on inner products between observations (the Gram matrix), one can avoid explicitly computing a large number of new features. This allows for a significant reduction in computational complexity from O(n^2*p^2 + n^3) to O(n^2*p). The text concludes by introducing the general concept of using a similarity measure k(x_i, x_j) directly, which is formalized in the subsequent section '1.4 Kernels'.

children.title: 1.4 Kernels
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.4 Kernels

children.title: 1.4.1 Examples of kernels
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.4 Kernels/1.4.1 Examples of kernels
children.summary: This page presents a mathematical proof regarding the properties of kernels, followed by Section 1.4.1 which provides examples of specific kernel functions. It details Proposition 4 concerning linear combinations and products of kernels, then defines and explains Linear, Polynomial, and Gaussian kernels with their respective formulas and properties.

children.title: 1.4.2 Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.4 Kernels/1.4.2 Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces
children.summary: This section defines Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS). It begins with Theorem 5, which states that for every kernel k, there exists a feature map φ into an inner product space H such that the kernel can be expressed as an inner product of the mapped features. A proof is provided by constructing the space H from functions formed by linear combinations of the kernel and defining an inner product on it. The text then discusses the completion of this space to form a Hilbert space and provides Definition 2 for an RKHS, where evaluation at any point x is a continuous linear functional represented by an inner product with a specific function k_x. Finally, examples of RKHS are given for the Linear kernel and the Sobolev kernel.

children.title: 1.4.3 The representer theorem
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.4 Kernels/1.4.3 The representer theorem
children.summary: This page presents section 1.4.3, titled 'The representer theorem,' which discusses the optimization problem in kernel ridge regression. It defines the objective function for ridge regression and states Theorem 6, attributed to Kimeldorf and Wahba (1970) and Schölkopf et al. (2001). The theorem establishes that minimizing a loss function over a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) is equivalent to minimizing a finite-dimensional quadratic form involving the kernel matrix. The page includes a detailed proof of this theorem using Pythagoras' theorem and concludes by applying the result to the specific case of the ridge regression objective.

children.title: 1.5 Kernel ridge regression
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.5 Kernel ridge regression
children.summary: This section introduces kernel ridge regression, a method that uses the kernel trick to solve potentially infinite-dimensional versions of ridge regression. It establishes a statistical framework for analyzing predictive performance by defining a data-generating process and assuming the true function lies within a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). The core of the section is Theorem 7, which provides an upper bound on the Mean Squared Prediction Error (MSPE) in terms of the eigenvalues of the kernel matrix. A detailed proof follows, utilizing techniques like the 'trace trick' and Hölder's inequality. The analysis is then extended to a random design setting using Mercer's theorem to describe the eigendecomposition of the kernel operator. Finally, it derives the optimal convergence rate for the error when using a Sobolev kernel.

children.title: 1.6 Other kernel machines
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.6 Other kernel machines

children.title: 1.6.1 The support vector machine
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.6 Other kernel machines/1.6.1 The support vector machine
children.summary: This section introduces the support vector machine (SVM) as a method for classification when data labels are discrete (e.g., {-1, 1}). It begins by defining the problem of finding a hyperplane that separates two classes. The text then formulates an optimization problem to find the hyperplane that maximizes the margin between these classes. It further extends this formulation to handle cases where classes are not perfectly separable by introducing a penalty term, leading to the standard SVM objective function. Finally, it generalizes the model to include a bias term (or translation), resulting in the final definition of the support vector classifier.

children.title: 1.6.2 Logistic regression
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.6 Other kernel machines/1.6.2 Logistic regression
children.summary: This page continues a discussion on Support Vector Machines (SVM) and introduces Logistic Regression. It presents the optimization problem for an SVM using a kernel matrix K, followed by the prediction formula. Section 1.6.2 details standard logistic regression, deriving its log-likelihood maximization problem and presenting its 'kernelised' version as an optimization over a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS).

children.title: 1.7 Large-scale kernel machines
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/1 Kernel machines/1.7 Large-scale kernel machines
children.summary: This section discusses methods for speeding up computations in large-scale kernel machines. It introduces the concept of random feature expansions to approximate kernels, thereby reducing computational complexity from cubic to linear in the number of data points. The text details how shift-invariant kernels can be approximated using Bochner's theorem and provides a concrete example using the Gaussian kernel.

sections.title: 2 Introduction to the Lasso
sections.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/2 Introduction to the Lasso

children.title: 2.1 Model selection
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/2 Introduction to the Lasso/2.1 Model selection
children.summary: The section '2.1 Model selection' revisits the linear model and discusses the Mean Squared Prediction Error (MSPE) of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). It explains that if the true set of relevant variables could be identified, a reduced model would yield a smaller MSPE and more accurate estimates. The text then introduces classical model selection strategies, starting with 'Best subset regression', which involves an exhaustive search over all possible subsets of explanatory variables. This method is noted to be computationally infeasible for large numbers of predictors (p > 50).

children.title: 2.2 The Lasso estimator
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/2 Introduction to the Lasso/2.2 The Lasso estimator

children.title: 2.2.1 Convexity and the Lasso
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/2 Introduction to the Lasso/2.2 The Lasso estimator/2.2.1 Convexity and the Lasso
children.summary: This page, titled 'Convexity and the Lasso', discusses the computational advantages of Lasso regression over Best subsets regression due to its convex optimization nature. It defines mathematical concepts of convex sets and functions, presents Proposition 9 regarding properties of convex functions (including conditions involving Hessians), and provides a proof for Proposition 10 demonstrating that Lasso fitted values are unique.

children.title: 2.2.2 Prediction error of the Lasso with no assumptions on the design
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/2 Introduction to the Lasso/2.2 The Lasso estimator/2.2.2 Prediction error of the Lasso with no assumptions on the design
children.summary: This section discusses the prediction error of the Lasso estimator when there are no assumptions on the design matrix, specifically in high-dimensional settings where p >> n. It presents Theorem 11, which establishes a bound on the prediction error with high probability under a normal linear model. The proof involves deriving an inequality based on the definition of the Lasso solution and utilizing Lemma 15 to bound the probability of a specific event.

children.title: 2.2.3 Concentration inequalities I
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/2 Introduction to the Lasso/2.2 The Lasso estimator/2.2.3 Concentration inequalities I
children.summary: This section, titled 'Concentration inequalities I', provides the theoretical foundation for bounding tail probabilities of random variables, which is necessary to prove Theorem 11. It begins by introducing Markov's inequality and deriving the Chernoff bound from it. The text then defines sub-Gaussian variables and presents key results: Hoeffding's lemma (showing bounded mean-zero variables are sub-Gaussian), a proposition on linear combinations of sub-Gaussian variables, and Lemma 15, which establishes a probability bound for the infinity norm of a vector of independent sub-Gaussian variables.

sections.title: 3 The Lasso and beyond
sections.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond

children.title: 3.1 Some facts from optimisation theory and convex analysis
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.1 Some facts from optimisation theory and convex analysis

children.title: 3.1.1 Subgradients
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.1 Some facts from optimisation theory and convex analysis/3.1.1 Subgradients
children.summary: The section titled '3.1.1 Subgradients' defines the concept of a subgradient for a convex function and introduces the subdifferential as the set of all such subgradients. It presents key propositions regarding subgradients, including their relationship to gradients when a function is differentiable, their behavior under scalar multiplication and addition, and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions for optimality. The section concludes by deriving the subdifferential of the ℓ₁-norm.

children.title: 3.1.2 The Lagrangian method
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.1 Some facts from optimisation theory and convex analysis/3.1.2 The Lagrangian method
children.summary: Section 3.1.2 introduces the Lagrangian method for solving constrained optimization problems of the form minimize f(x) subject to g(x)=0. It defines the Lagrangian function L(x, θ) = f(x) + θ^T g(x) and explains that the method involves finding a parameter θ* such that the minimizer x* of the Lagrangian satisfies the original constraint g(x*)=0.

children.title: 3.2 Lasso solutions
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.2 Lasso solutions
children.summary: Section 3.2 characterizes the solutions to the Lasso problem using tools from convex analysis. It states that a vector is a Lasso solution if and only if it satisfies specific Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, which are expressed as an equation involving the transpose of the design matrix X, the response vector Y, and a subgradient vector with an infinity norm less than or equal to 1.

children.title: 3.3 Variable selection
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.3 Variable selection
children.summary: This section discusses variable selection in the context of a noiseless high-dimensional linear model. It presents Theorem 20, which establishes conditions under which a Lasso solution correctly recovers the sign pattern of the true coefficient vector. A key condition mentioned is the 'irrepresentable condition' (||Δ||_∞ ≤ 1), which ensures that variables not in the true support set do not correlate too strongly with those in the support set.

children.title: 3.4 Prediction and estimation
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.4 Prediction and estimation
children.summary: This section, titled 'Prediction and estimation', introduces the compatibility condition as a requirement for obtaining Mean Squared Prediction Error (MSPE) bounds for the Lasso estimator. It defines the compatibility constant φ² via an infimum over a restricted set of vectors. Theorem 21 is then presented, which provides a high-probability bound on the prediction error and estimation error of the Lasso solution under this condition. The proof involves deriving a series of inequalities based on the basic inequality and Hölder's inequality. The section concludes by beginning to discuss the strength of the compatibility condition in relation to the population covariance matrix.

children.title: 3.5 The compatibility condition
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.5 The compatibility condition

children.title: 3.5.1 Concentration inequalities II
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.5 The compatibility condition/3.5.1 Concentration inequalities II
children.summary: This page presents a mathematical discussion on concentration inequalities, specifically focusing on Bernstein's inequality. It begins by defining Bernstein's condition for a random variable and then states Proposition 23, which provides tail bounds for the sum of independent random variables satisfying this condition. The page concludes with a detailed proof of the proposition using moment generating functions and the Chernoff method.

children.title: 3.5.2 The compatibility condition and random design
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.5 The compatibility condition/3.5.2 The compatibility condition and random design
children.summary: This page contains a mathematical proof for Lemma 24 regarding the product of mean-zero sub-Gaussian random variables satisfying Bernstein's condition. It includes detailed derivations using Fubini's theorem, Jensen's inequality, and Cauchy-Schwarz. The page also introduces section 3.5.2 on 'The compatibility condition and random design' and presents Theorem 25 concerning asymptotic frameworks for design matrices.

children.title: 3.6 Computation
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.6 Computation
children.summary: This page contains a mathematical proof concluding with Corollary 26, followed by Section 3.6 titled 'Computation'. The section discusses the coordinate descent optimization technique for computing Lasso solutions, presenting the general function form and the iterative update equations used in the algorithm. It references Tseng [2001] regarding convergence properties and concludes with Corollary 27.

children.title: 3.7 Extensions of the Lasso
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.7 Extensions of the Lasso

children.title: 3.7.1 Structural penalties
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.7 Extensions of the Lasso/3.7.1 Structural penalties
children.summary: This page contains a mathematical proof regarding the convergence of a minimizer for a continuous function, referencing the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem and Tseng [2001]. It then details an algorithmic strategy using coordinate descent with a 'warm start' to solve the Lasso on a grid of lambda values. The text concludes with section 3.7, discussing extensions of the Lasso to other loss functions like logistic regression, and section 3.7.1, which introduces structural penalties.

children.title: 3.7.2 Reducing the bias of the Lasso
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/3 The Lasso and beyond/3.7 Extensions of the Lasso/3.7.2 Reducing the bias of the Lasso
children.summary: This section discusses methods to reduce the bias inherent in the Lasso estimator, which shrinks non-zero coefficients towards zero. It introduces two primary approaches: re-estimation techniques like the 'relaxed Lasso' (Meinshausen, 2007) and the 'adaptive Lasso' (Zou, 2006), which uses weighted regression based on an initial estimate. Additionally, it covers the use of non-convex penalty functions, such as the 'minimax concave penalty' (MCP) by Zhang (2010), noting that while these can mitigate bias, they may introduce multiple local minima that complicate optimization.

sections.title: 4 Graphical modelling and causal inference
sections.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference

children.title: 4.1 Graphs
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.1 Graphs
children.summary: Section 4.1 introduces the fundamental concepts of graphs used in graphical modelling and causal inference. It defines a graph as a pair of vertices (nodes) and edges, specifically indexing them by random variables. The section details types of edges (directed vs. undirected), adjacency, subgraphs, parent-child relationships, v-structures, skeletons, paths, descendants, colliders, directed cycles, and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). It concludes with definitions for blocked paths and d-separation within DAGs.

children.title: 4.2 Conditional independence graphs
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.2 Conditional independence graphs
children.summary: This page contains mathematical definitions and proofs related to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and conditional independence. It begins with the definition of a moralised graph and Definition 8 regarding topological orderings, followed by Proposition 28 which states that every DAG has a topological ordering along with its proof. The page then introduces Section 4.2 on Conditional Independence Graphs, defining conditional independence (Definition 9) and the conditional independence graph (CIG) (Definition 10).

children.title: 4.3 Gaussian graphical models
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.3 Gaussian graphical models

children.title: 4.3.1 Normal conditionals
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.3 Gaussian graphical models/4.3.1 Normal conditionals
children.summary: Section 4.3.1 Normal conditionals presents Proposition 29, which defines the conditional distribution of a subset of variables $Z_A$ given another subset $Z_B = z_B$ for a multivariate Gaussian vector $Z$. The section includes a proof demonstrating that by constructing an independent component $Z_A - MZ_B$, one can derive the mean and variance of the resulting normal distribution.

children.title: 4.3.2 Nodewise regression
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.3 Gaussian graphical models/4.3.2 Nodewise regression
children.summary: Section 4.3.2, titled 'Nodewise regression', specializes the previously discussed normal conditionals to the specific case where a single variable $Z_k$ is conditioned on all other variables $Z_{-k}$. It derives the resulting linear regression equation for $Z_k$, defining the intercept term $m_k$ and the conditional distribution of the error term $\varepsilon_k$.

children.title: 4.3.3 The precision matrix and conditional independence
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.3 Gaussian graphical models/4.3.3 The precision matrix and conditional independence
children.summary: This page discusses statistical methods for estimating Conditional Independence Graphs (CIG), specifically focusing on neighborhood selection using the Lasso and the relationship between precision matrices and conditional independence. It details the 'OR' and 'AND' rules for edge selection in CIG estimation and presents Proposition 30 regarding blockwise inversion of symmetric positive definite matrices to interpret mean and variance.

children.title: 4.3.4 The Graphical Lasso
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.3 Gaussian graphical models/4.3.4 The Graphical Lasso
children.summary: This page presents a mathematical derivation for the Graphical Lasso method, starting with the density function of a multivariate normal distribution. It defines the log-likelihood and sample statistics (mean and covariance), then algebraically manipulates these terms to derive the maximum likelihood estimate for the precision matrix Omega.

children.title: 4.4 Structural equation models
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.4 Structural equation models
children.summary: This page continues a discussion on statistical modeling, specifically focusing on the graphical Lasso method for estimating precision matrices and sparse conditional independence graphs. It then introduces Section 4.4, 'Structural equation models' (SEMs), defining them as collections of equations representing data-generating processes using directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). The section concludes with Example 4.4.1, which presents an artificial SEM involving variables related to taking a course, attending a statistical modeling class, and hearing about machine learning.

children.title: 4.5 Interventions
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.5 Interventions
children.summary: This page discusses interventions in Structural Equation Models (SEM), specifically focusing on how replacing structural equations affects the joint law of variables. It defines a 'perfect intervention' using the do-operator notation and provides a continued example (4.4.1) where variable Z2 is set to 1. The text includes mathematical derivations comparing the probability of Z1=1 under an intervention versus conditional expectation, showing they are not equal.

children.title: 4.6 The Markov properties on DAGs
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.6 The Markov properties on DAGs
children.summary: Section 4.6 introduces the Markov properties on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) in the context of Structural Equation Models (SEMs). It defines two key properties: the Markov factorisation property, which relates the joint density to a product of conditional densities based on parent nodes, and the global Markov property, which links d-separation in the graph to conditional independence in the probability distribution. The section states that these properties are equivalent for distributions with a density (Theorem 31) and asserts that the law of an SEM obeys the Markov factorisation property (Proposition 32). It concludes by noting that these properties allow one to read information about the distribution from the DAG and determine the effects of interventions.

children.title: 4.7 Causal structure learning
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.7 Causal structure learning

children.title: 4.7.1 Three obstacles
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.7 Causal structure learning/4.7.1 Three obstacles
children.summary: The section titled '4.7.1 Three obstacles' introduces the challenges in causal structure learning. It states that there are three specific obstacles to this process, noting that the first two are more immediate while the third is somewhat subtle.

children.title: 4.7.2 The PC algorithm
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.7 Causal structure learning/4.7.2 The PC algorithm

children.title: Population version
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.7 Causal structure learning/4.7.2 The PC algorithm/Population version
children.summary: This page details the 'Population version' of the PC algorithm, a method for learning causal structures from data. It introduces Algorithm 1, which finds the skeleton of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) by iteratively removing edges based on conditional independence tests. The text also presents Algorithm 2, which identifies v-structures to orient the remaining edges in the graph.

children.title: Sample version
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.7 Causal structure learning/4.7.2 The PC algorithm/Sample version
children.summary: This page describes the sample version of the PC algorithm, which uses conditional independence tests on data rather than direct queries. It explains that if data is multivariate normal, sample partial correlation can be used to test for conditional independence, providing a mathematical formula for this condition. The text concludes by outlining the computational method: regressing variables X_j and X_k on X_S and computing the correlation between the resulting residuals.

children.title: Chapter 5
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.7 Causal structure learning/4.7.2 The PC algorithm/Chapter 5
children.summary: This section introduces high-dimensional inference, focusing on the limitations of standard estimators like the Lasso in settings where the number of predictors (p) exceeds the sample size (n). It discusses the development of the 'debiased Lasso' as a method to perform valid statistical inference. The text details the mathematical derivation of this estimator, starting from the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions of the Lasso and constructing an approximate inverse of the covariance matrix to correct for bias.

children.title: Theorem 36.
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/4 Graphical modelling and causal inference/4.7 Causal structure learning/4.7.2 The PC algorithm/Theorem 36.
children.summary: This page presents a mathematical proof for Theorem 36, which establishes asymptotic properties of an estimator in a high-dimensional statistical setting. It defines sparsity measures and sets up an asymptotic regime where the number of variables $p$ and sample size $n$ grow to infinity. The proof relies on Theorem 21 and derives bounds for the estimation error of coefficients ($\hat{\beta} - \beta^0$) and variance estimates ($\hat{\tau}_j^2$).

children.title: 5.1 Using the debiased Lasso in practice
children.path: Statistical Learning Notes.pdf/5 High-dimensional inference/5.1 Using the debiased Lasso in practice
children.summary: This section explains the practical application of the debiased Lasso method. It derives an approximate normal distribution for the estimator, which is then used to construct (1-α)-level confidence intervals. The text notes that the only unknown parameter in these intervals, σ, can be estimated using methods like the square-root or scaled Lasso.
